Thomas Pynchon. Born in 1937, an American novelist of legendary reclusion whose encyclopedic, labyrinthine novels treat entropy, paranoia, and systems breakdown as the condition of postmodern consciousness. His masterwork, Gravity's Rainbow, published in 1973, is a canonical difficult postmodern text. His oeuvre probes the intersections of history, technology, physics, and narrative, all rendered in darkly comic, digressive prose bristling with footnotes and temporal jumps.

Gravity's Rainbow follows Tyrone Slothrop in World War II, ostensibly tracing a rocket's trajectory but actually mapping the paranoid consciousness of wartime and the dawning nuclear age. The novel resists linear reading and conventional plot. Pynchon is a notoriously private author who has never been photographed and grants no interviews. His invisibility has become part of his literary mythology. He employs metafiction, anachrony, and paranoid hermeneutics. His novels position readers as detective-interpreters searching for patterns that may or may not exist. His early story Entropy uses the physical law of entropy—the increase of disorder—as a metaphor for meaning-collapse and information decay in human systems. Other major novels include The Crying of Lot 49, published in 1966, a short postmodern mystery, and Against the Day, published in 2006, another encyclopedic historical epic. Pynchon's work is notoriously difficult, allusive, and technical. Reading Pynchon is treated as an intellectual challenge. His novels resist paraphrase and demand rereading. Don DeLillo shares Pynchon's postmodern obsession with paranoia, entropy, and systems theory, as does David Foster Wallace, who explicitly references Pynchon and shares his interest in information overload and narrative difficulty.
